name: Ben Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me, Ben. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, what's a normal working day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a big excavator at the lithium mine, loading haul trucks at the face. Every pass, four buckets a truck, and you try to keep the floor flat and the trucks never waiting. I've been there fourteen months. Before that I had my own landscaping business for nine years, until two big clients didn't pay and it went under, so I came to the mine to pay off what we owed.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like and what grinds you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the machine, honestly, it's like the mini-digger I had, times fifty. I use the AI every day: I photograph pages of the operator manual and get it to quiz me on the bus, and I ask it why my cycle times are slower than the guy on the other shift. What grinds me is being the junior at forty-three after being my own boss, and the debt. Lucia works the front desk at the town council, and between us we're still paying off the business and the mortgage, so there's nothing in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, good, that's what I thought, it's a great tool and not much more. I'd probably say it online too, I post a fair bit in the local business groups. People know I'm a bit of a fan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, nothing much changes, which is fine. I keep using it to learn faster and get off the junior rate sooner. Honestly I'd be a little disappointed, I like the stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down, get my cycle times up and aim to be signed off on the bigger shovel within the year. I'd keep paying down the business debt, about three hundred a month. And I'd keep using the AI to study, it's how I've caught up as fast as I have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a bit of disappointment, if that makes sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why disappointed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I like a new tool. When I had the landscaping business, I was the first in town with a laser level and a design app, and it won me jobs. I'd have liked to see what this stuff could really do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened when the business went under?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two builders owed me twenty-two thousand between them and both went bust. I had to sell the trucks and the mini-digger. Lucia never said I told you so, which I'll love her for till I die.

S0.say: He'd say AI is a great tool and not much more, including online in local business groups where people know he's a fan.
S0.think: He thinks little changes for him and he'd keep using AI to learn faster and get off the junior rate. He admits he'd be a little disappointed.
S0.do: Works to improve his cycle times and get signed off on the bigger shovel within a year. Pays about three hundred a month off the old business debt and keeps studying with AI.
S0.quote: Lucia never said I told you so, which I'll love her for till I die.
S0.fieldNote: Ben is a former business owner who likes new tools and uses AI daily to catch up at work. His main financial weight is old business debt. In the calm picture, his only feeling is mild disappointment that the technology didn't go further.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is progress, and progress has always made some jobs smaller and others bigger. People should get going and learn, not wait to be rescued. I'd say it at work and online, and some guys wouldn't like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the excavators get remote control and then self-driving within a few years, the trucks are already halfway there. That doesn't scare me much, because I'd want to be the person who runs three of them from a desk. I've changed careers once already, I can do it again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to be on any trial of remote shovels and put in for the autonomy training the moment it's posted. I'd use AI to learn the control software before the course even starts. On weekends I'd pick up small landscaping jobs with a hired mini-digger, because there's always demand and it brings in a bit extra.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, even a bit excited. Like the first spring of the business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said some guys wouldn't like what you'd say. Who?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older operators, mostly. They've got thirty years on the shovels and they hate the screens. I get it, but I'd say to them, you can be angry or you can be in the chair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Lucia's job at the council?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the one I'd worry about, actually. A lot of front desk work is forms and questions, and that's exactly what the AI does. I'd sit with her and help her learn the tools so she's the one running them.

S1.say: He'd call it progress that shrinks some jobs and grows others, and urge people to learn rather than wait to be rescued, knowing some workmates would dislike that.
S1.think: He thinks excavators will go remote and then self-driving within a few years, but he wants to run several from a desk. Having changed careers once, he's confident he can again.
S1.do: Volunteers for remote shovel trials and applies for autonomy training immediately, learning the software with AI in advance. Takes weekend landscaping jobs with a hired mini-digger for extra income and helps Lucia learn AI tools.
S1.feel: Calm and a little excited, like the first spring of his business.
S1.quote: I get it, but I'd say to them, you can be angry or you can be in the chair.
S1.fieldNote: Ben sees gradual automation as a chance and moves first, in line with his free-market views about self-reliance. His concern shifts to his partner's council job, which is more exposed to thinking AI. A weekend side income draws on his old trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a massive shake-up and people need to move fast. I'd still say get learning and get working, not sit at home. But I'd admit two years is brutal, even for someone like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the desk job I was aiming for might not last either, if the AI can run the fleet itself. And we've got nothing saved and a debt from the business. I'm good at changing, but changing costs money, and we haven't got any.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go back to landscaping on the side straight away, maybe full-time, because people's gardens might be the last thing a robot gets to cheaply. I'd use AI to run the bookings, quotes and marketing, so it's just me and a hired machine. We'd cut everything, and I'd ask the bank to pause the business debt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd feel the pressure every day, but I'd still feel like I was driving, not being driven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've been your own boss before and it didn't work out. Why try again?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I learned more from that than from anything. The business failed because two clients didn't pay, not because the work dried up. This time I'd take deposits up front and keep it small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Mateo and Eva?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them Dad's going back to gardens, and they can help on Saturdays for pocket money. Mateo's thirteen, he'd roll his eyes but he'd come. I'd want them to see that you get back up.

S2.say: He'd call it a massive shake-up and still urge people to keep learning and working, while admitting two years is brutal even for him.
S2.think: He thinks the desk role he was aiming for might also vanish. With no savings and leftover business debt, he notes that changing costs money he doesn't have.
S2.do: Restarts landscaping on the side straight away, possibly full-time, using AI for bookings, quotes and marketing. Cuts all spending and asks the bank to pause the old business debt.
S2.feel: Anxious and under pressure, but still feeling in control.
S2.quote: I'm good at changing, but changing costs money, and we haven't got any.
S2.fieldNote: This picture tests Ben's confidence because his planned path disappears and his debts limit his options. He falls back on his old trade, now run with AI, and has learned lessons from his business failure. He still feels in control, which sets him apart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a decent runway, so there's no excuse not to get ready. I'd tell the young guys on the crew to learn the new machines and a second skill. I'd say the government should keep out of the way and let people get on with it, maybe help with apprenticeships.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, I'd get onto the remote shovels, pay off the old debt and get the landscaping going on weekends. By the time it all hits I'd have something of my own again. I'd be forty-eight, which isn't too old to run a small business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year: autonomy training, and clear the business debt with any overtime. Second year: start weekend landscaping properly, with AI doing the admin. By year three or four, think about buying a small robot mower or two, if they're cheap, so the business can grow without me needing to hire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a good way. Busy, with a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Buying robots for your own business. Isn't that the same thing you're worried about at the mine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, and I've thought about it. But if robots are coming either way, I'd rather own one than be replaced by one. That's just the way it works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Lucia feel about you starting a business again?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, and fair enough. I'd have to show her the numbers every month, which I'd do with a spreadsheet the AI builds for me. And I wouldn't quit the mine until the business was paying.

S3.say: He'd call five years a decent runway, urge younger crewmates to learn new machines and a second skill, and say government should mostly stay out of the way apart from helping with apprenticeships.
S3.think: He thinks five years lets him move to remote shovels, clear his debt and rebuild his landscaping business. He'd be forty-eight, which he doesn't see as too old to run a small business.
S3.do: Takes autonomy training and clears the business debt with overtime in year one. Restarts weekend landscaping in year two with AI handling admin, and considers buying a small robot mower or two by year three or four.
S3.feel: Uneasy in a good way, busy and with a plan.
S3.quote: But if robots are coming either way, I'd rather own one than be replaced by one.
S3.fieldNote: Ben treats the five-year warning as a business runway, with clear steps year by year. He resolves the contradiction of using robots himself through a belief in ownership. He's careful to take his partner's worries into account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, and it's on each of us to use it. Learn, save, build something. I'd also say families should stick together, that's what gets people through big changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I think I'd come out of it better than I am now. Run the remote fleet for a while, pay off everything, and then grow the landscaping into a proper business with a couple of robots and a couple of people. The kids would be grown, and maybe Mateo works with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd follow the same plan as the five-year picture, just slower, without wrecking myself or the family. Debt cleared in two years, weekend business by year three, then invest the savings into machines once I'm sure it pays. I'd keep using AI for everything from study to bookkeeping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly. Ten years is enough for a man to build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for Mateo and Eva in that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want Mateo to learn a trade and how to run a business, because those two together are hard to replace. Eva's eight and wants to be a vet this week, an astronaut last week. Whatever she picks, I'd want her to know how to use the tools, not be scared of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the ten-year picture that still bothers you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What happens to the guys who don't want to change, like the older operators. Some of them will be fine, but some will just sit at home. That's not a life, and it worries me for the town.

S4.say: He'd say ten years is plenty and it's on each person to learn, save and build something, adding that families sticking together gets people through big changes.
S4.think: He thinks he'd come out better than now: running the remote fleet, clearing his debts and growing his landscaping into a proper business with robots and staff. His children would be grown and his son might join him.
S4.do: Follows a slower version of his five-year plan: debt cleared in two years and the weekend business running by year three. Then invests savings in machines once he's sure it pays, using AI for study and bookkeeping throughout.
S4.feel: Calm; ten years feels like enough to build something.
S4.quote: Eva's eight and wants to be a vet this week, an astronaut last week.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Ben expects to be better off and is genuinely calm. His worry shifts to older colleagues who won't adapt and what that means for the town. His traditional values show in family, self-reliance and ownership.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I wouldn't have the money or the time to get my feet under me, and the debt would still be sitting there. What would help is a pause on old business debts and some cheap start-up loans for small trades businesses. I don't need someone to look after me, I need a bit of room to move.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about failing. I failed once, properly, lost the trucks and nearly the house. It taught me that the worst thing isn't failing, it's sitting still while it happens to you.

headlineQuote: It taught me that the worst thing isn't failing, it's sitting still while it happens to you.
portrait: Ben Novak is a 43-year-old excavator operator at a large open-pit lithium mine, fourteen months in after his landscaping business failed when two clients didn't pay. He and his partner Lucia, who works the front desk at the town council, are still paying off that debt with no savings. He uses AI every day to study and sees automation as progress, believing in self-reliance, family and ownership. He stays calm in the slower pictures and becomes anxious but still in control in the two-year AGI picture, falling back on landscaping. With more time he plans to clear his debt and rebuild a small business that owns its own robots.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because he wouldn't have the money or time to get established and the old business debt would still be there.
whatWouldHelp: A pause on old business debts and cheap start-up loans for small trades businesses, giving him room to move rather than being looked after.
